newsitem.title: MALI: Mali - cradle of old African empire built on gold.
newsitem.headline: Mali - cradle of old African empire built on gold.

text.p: Mali, which on Sunday kicked off its second multi-party elections since independence, was the cradle of an African empire which was built on gold and flourished during Europe's Middle Ages.
Today, the sprawling West African nation is one of the poorest on earth, struggling against drought and the advance of the Sahara desert.
Malians heading for the bright lights of Europe are at the heart of former colonial power France's fight to halt illegal immigration from the world's poorest continent.

But after a successful transition from one-party rule to democracy in 1992, an economic liberalisation programme that has won plaudits from the World Bank and lively foreign interest in its gold, the future is starting to look more promising.

Word of the wealth of the mighty 13th and 14th Century empire of Mali, from which the modern Mali took its name after independence in 1960, captured the imagination of the rich and powerful in Europe.
When Mansa (ruler) Moussa made a pilgrimage to Mecca in the 14th Century, he took eight tonnes of gold which he liberally dispensed in Cairo causing the price of the metal to collapse.
Some historians say it was talk of the wealth of the Malian city of Jenne which brought the first European explorers -- the Portuguese -- and their ships to the coast of West Africa.
Mali's independence leader Modibo Keita steered the country on a radical, pro-Soviet, one-party course until his removal in 1968 by young army officers led by Moussa Traore.
Mali embraced multi-party democracy after the army ousted Traore in 1991 following violent pro-democracy demonstrations in which more than 200 people were killed.
A transitional military government led by Amadou Toumani Toure stepped down after elections won by historian Alpha Oumar Konare and his Alliance for Democracy in Mali (ADEMA) party.

Light-skinned Tuaregs -- who controlled the Middle Ages caravan routes across the Sahara -- took up arms against the black-dominated government in 1990. Mali sealed peace in 1996 with a huge bonfire of weapons in the ancient city of Timbuktu.
On the economic front, the World Bank predicts that Mali will be Africa's third largest gold exporter by 1998.

But its 11 million people remain poor with a per capita annual income of just $250. The average life expectancy is 46, just 17 percent of adults can read and write and and only 37 percent have access to safe water, according to U.N. estimates.
Mali held parliamentary elections on Sunday. It holds a presidential poll on May 4 and local elections on June 1.
